modern:
At first tragedies were brought on the stage as a means of reminding men of the things that happen to them, and that it is according to nature for things to happen so, and that, if you are delighted with what is shown on the stage, you should not be troubled by what takes place on the larger stage. For you see that these things must be accomplished in this way, and that even those who cry out “O Cithaeron” have to bear them. And indeed, some things are said well by the dramatic writers, such as this one especially:—

“Me and my children if the gods neglect,
This has its reason too.”

And again,—

“We must not chafe and fret at what happens.”

And,—

“Reap life’s harvest like the wheat’s fruitful ear.”

And other things of the same kind.

After tragedy the old comedy was introduced, which had a magisterial freedom of speech, and by its very plain speaking was useful in reminding men to beware of insolence; and for this purpose Diogenes too used to borrow from these writers.

But as to the middle comedy, which came next, observe what it was, and again, for what purpose the new comedy was introduced, which gradually sank into a mere imitative artifice. That some good things are said even by these writers, everybody knows: but the whole design of such poetry and drama, what end does it look to?

At first tragedies were brought on the stage as means of reminding men of the things which happen to them, and that it is according to nature for things to happen so, and that, if you are delighted with what is shown on the stage, you should not be troubled with that which takes place on the larger stage. For you see that these things must be accomplished thus, and that even they bear them who cry out, “O Cithaeron.” And, indeed, some things are said well by the dramatic writers, of which kind is the following especially:—

“Me and my children if the gods neglect,
This has its reason too.”

And again,—

“We must not chafe and fret at that which happens.”

And,—

“Life’s harvest reap like the wheat’s fruitful ear.”

And other things of the same kind.

After tragedy the old comedy was introduced, which had a magisterial freedom of speech, and by its very plainness of speaking was useful in reminding men to beware of insolence; and for this purpose too Diogenes used to take from these writers.

But as to the middle comedy, which came next, observe what it was, and again, for what object the new comedy was introduced, which gradually sank down into a mere mimic artifice. That some good things are said even by these writers, everybody knows: but the whole plan of such poetry and dramaturgy, to what end does it look?

explained.summary:
Marcus asks what drama is actually for. The early tragedies, he thinks, showed people that suffering is a normal part of life: if you can watch disaster on stage, you can bear it on the bigger stage of real life. Even Oedipus, crying out to the mountain where he was abandoned as a baby, had to endure his fate. He picks out lines from the playwrights that say just that.

The old comedy did a different job, mocking the arrogant so frankly that it kept people humble, and Diogenes the Cynic borrowed from it. The later comedies drifted into mere clever imitation. Some good lines survive in them, but he wants to know what any entertainment is ultimately aiming at.
explained.today: It’s a fair question to ask of a box set or a podcast. Some films leave you better able to face grief or failure, and some satire takes the powerful down a peg. Plenty of what we watch is just skilful filler, and it’s worth noticing which is which before the next episode autoplays.
